Honorable mention

HVRACAN

Our honorable mention comes from relative newcomer to the Latin Trap scene, Young Chimi (stylized as YOVNGCHIMI). This soaring track is propelled by the kinetic energy of the beat and the effortless nature, if somewhat monotone delivery, of Chimi. A song almost intentionally written to push one further on a long run is somewhat undone by the intensely grating intro by DJ Khaled—who insists on spouting nonsense before the fun can even begin.

Now, the countdown
10

No. 10

Flame

At number 10, this Falcons and Stush collaboration hits like a shot of espresso condensed in under 3-minutes of playtime. This slight but memorable track is pure energy but is at times made less satisfying by the listener's general inability to make out approximately 60% of what Stush is ultimately saying on the track.

9

No. 9

Sleepwalker

A list like this was always going to include an obligatory "screamy" song, and while quite tame in comparison to band President's colleagues in the genre, this song delivers an anthemic though at times heavy dose of energy and hopelessness in equal measure. If you ask me, that's a perfect combination for a marathon.

8

No. 8

6 Foot 7 Foot

The first of two "throwbacks" on this list, Lil Wayne's seminal 6 foot 7 foot is a master class in attitude and braggadocio. Wayne's delivery oozes a confidence that is contagious even to those uninitiated to Lil Wayne's lyrical wizardry. I'm not saying lasagna saw a resurgence after this song dropped, but I'm also not not saying that.

Open in Spotify ↗
7

No. 7

Ladders

As we quickly approach 10 years since Mac Miller's unexpected and untimely passing, it feels like only yesterday that I first heard Ladders. Somewhere between the funky bass riffs and sharp horns as well as Miller's witty delivery is a pure energy that makes you want to move. Its placement on this list at number 7 is both an homage to it appearing as track 7 on his final album (while alive), but also appropriate in the context of this list as it might make a marathon runner want to dance instead of run.

Open in Spotify ↗
6

No. 6

Tití Me Preguntó

By the time Tití Me Preguntó (TMP) dropped, Benito Ocasio (aka Bad Bunny) was already a household name. But it's perhaps this track—and as part of the broader Un Verano Sin Ti album package—that Bad Bunny's fame went beyond the stratosphere. TMP in particular became synonymous with the driving energy that good workouts are made of. Despite its placement at number 6, catch me on a different day and it would crack the top 3.

Open in Spotify ↗
5

No. 5

Mercy

At 5 minutes and 29 seconds, the song that cracks our Top 5 is the second of our two throwbacks on this list. Originally released in 2012, Mercy features verses from a staggering 4 rappers who each insist on bodying the track. Whether or not you think 2 Chainz's verse "I'm drunk and high at the same time drinkin champagne on the airplane" is actually punctuated by the ad lib "travel" rather than "tell em", one thing is for certain: this song is 5 minutes of nonstop gas.

Open in Spotify ↗
4

No. 4

Dance Now

At number 4, you'd be hard pressed to not consider Atlanta rapper JID's hit song Dance Now an exercise in lyrical showmanship. However, its deep bass and the memorable hook give the song a melodic and forward driving appeal that is often lost in tracks by other "lyrical miracle"-type rappers who favor complexity over good vibes. JID does both with ease.

Open in Spotify ↗
3

No. 3

Ace Trumpets

Easily two of the best rappers of all-time, real-life brothers Pusha-T and Malice returned after a 16 year hiatus to retake the mantle of legendary rap duo, Clipse. The first single, Ace Trumpets, off their new album features punishing bass loops and intricate rhyme schemes, drenched in an unmatched bravado that makes anyone listening (especially while doing physical activity) scientifically stronger and faster. In at least three countries this song is banned as a performance enhancing drug.

Open in Spotify ↗
2

No. 2

Wassup

What do Young Miko and Lil Wayne have in common—other than stage monikers that imply a physically slight persona? Young Miko's "Wassup" borrows Wayne's distinctive Lollipop beat interpolation, while simultaneously making it completely her own. Miko's relative nascency to the scene might make her a surprising pick for runner-up to my pick for "Marathon playlist contribution", but it's precisely this kind of kick-the-door-in energy laced with Young Miko's confident—bordering on the casual—delivery that makes this an energizing beast of a track. Just make sure that as you pass others in the race, you say wassup.

And now, the one I'd put first.

1

No. 1

Voy a llevarte a PR

Where Miko's placement at number 2 was likely surprising, our number 1 spot really shouldn't be. The only artist named twice on this list, Bad Bunny is at this point a genre unto his own. Winner of the 2026 Album of the Year Grammy, Benito's fun yet deeply personal homage to Puerto Rico is musical excellence from top to bottom. But, perhaps no song on the album comes through with as much energy and driving power as "Voy a llevarte pa PR", a slick instant classic reggeaton banger that refuses to let up until the last second. At this point, I've listened to this song hundreds of times and it comfortably sits as one of my favorites from Mr. Ocasio. It's a delight from start to finish; pure energy dynamite. It truly represents and embodies the kind of fire I'd like to contribute to the other tracks on the marathon playlist.
